extracted.intended_audience: scholars and readers of classical/medieval natural history, lapidary work, and materia medica (Latin readers, historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting descriptive criteria and classificatory rules from a Latin natural-history treatise on stones (lapidary) and plants, including observational/experimental guidance and materia medica remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetism: pole structure and attraction/repulsion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnet is described as having two parts/poles; one part directs iron toward the boreal (north) and the other toward the austral (south). Which part of the magnet contacts the iron determines whether the iron is attracted or repelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual guidance and experimental notes: similar things attract and dissimilar repel; if an iron piece contacts the magnet at the pole that tends to the austral, that iron may be propelled toward the austral or repelled depending on which magnet part it meets; small experiments with pyxis lines and iron on tables demonstrate how the magnet beneath a board causes movement of iron above it; constructions (statues, rods) with concealed magnets are proposed to produce apparent animation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental testing of a stone's action on flesh
rubrics_metrics.description: To test medicinal or wondrous effects of certain stones, observe whether contact/penetration causes pain, bleeding, and subsequent healing or not; note the size of wounds/bleeding and any secreted fluids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example experiment recounted: a small white bean-like stone allegedly penetrated flesh without pain and left only a tiny drop of blood and no lasting wound. Observers are advised to monitor pain sensation, presence/absence of blood or wound, later inflammation or healing, and to consider confounding factors (skin fat, needle curvature, depth). Remedies applied (oils, resins) and their effects are also recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories of stone formation (generation/growth vs accretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two modes of stone increase are proposed: (1) addition by veins or external material accreting onto a stone (nutritive accession), and (2) internal generation analogous to the development of a chick in an egg—an intrinsic growth from an initial seed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency/opacity and behavior under fire/cold are diagnostic: clear (crystalline) stones are thought to be water-based and formed by cold, therefore dissolve by fire; opaque stones may have other origins. Examples: crystal is pure/transparent and thus water-concreted; silex is 'cerreus' and dissolves by fire because it was congealed by cold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gem valuation and quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Stones and gems are valued according to hardness, density (weight), polish/luster, color, and rarity; denser and harder materials take and retain a higher polish and are considered more splendid and valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance notes: polishing increases splendour; dense/hard materials (e.g., adamas among stones, analogous remarks for metals and woods) command higher price. The text links polish, density, and fineness with higher market value and notes that some soft stones can be made to appear more precious by work, but true value attaches to intrinsic hardness/density and uniform appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting fake or composite gems
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for recognizing forgeries include checking for seams, heterogeneous parts joined together, mismatches in weight/polish/color, artificial armatures or gilding, and unnatural uniformity or signs of assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and tests: pearls sometimes fabricated by joining shell pieces; some armatures or external gildings produce a false sheen; testing in fire or by abrasion (polishing/filing) may reveal base material; look for seams where material was added. The text warns of deceptive artifices used to cheat buyers (gold leaf, assembly of shells, false armature beneath polish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of plants into genera (trees/herbs/shrubs/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants are classed into four principal genera—trees (arbores), herbs (herbae), with mention of intermediate or additional kinds (e.g., frutices/shrubs or a fifth intermediate type). The classification is based on growth form such as presence of a persistent trunk, overall height, and stem characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: a tree is a plant whose stem/trunk renews/grows to a considerable size (e.g., pear tree), whereas herbs have stems that do not attain great size and may live only a few years; a possible fifth intermediate genus occurs when a plant is sometimes tree-like and sometimes herb-like (examples given such as ruta). The author describes how art (cultivation/grafting) can modify stature (trees made herb-like and vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for distinguishing species of plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Species differentiation should be based on odor, taste (flavor), sap/juices, morphology of leaves/flowers/fruits, perennial vs annual habit, evergreen vs deciduous nature, and root/trunk characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: odor and taste often indicate medicinal properties and help group species (e.g., fraxinus vs diptamus); the same outward form may hide differing virtues, so scent, flavor, and sap must be tested. Regional variants should be noted but core species identity relies on the cited characters. Use Dioscorides as an authority and test multiple characters rather than names alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of region, soil, and transplanting on plant properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant's properties (appearance, virtues, odor, flavor, fruiting) can vary with region, soil, climate, and whether it is transplanted; transplanted plants may change some traits while retaining core nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: transplanting trees/herbs to new soils or climates can produce plants that appear as new varieties; some plants only grow in certain regions or under certain climatic conditions (e.g., some species are confined to cold provinces); cultivation and art can alter stature and fruitfulness (pomegranate, quince, peach cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapidary materials and abrasive/polishing agents and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain minerals and materials (pumex, smiris, obsidian, talc, gypsum, pumex-like stones) serve as abrasives, polishers, or have specific working properties (light, tenacious, glutinous, resistant to water/heat) relevant to finishing gems and making tablets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and uses from the text: pumex and smiris used to polish and clean gems; talchum (talc-like) behaves like glass and can be used like speculum; gypsum and related earths used in building and for varnishes; some stones are used to make durable writing tablets or to make inscriptions by polishing. The text also notes which materials resist fire and water and which are friable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant anatomy vocabulary and parts useful for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: List and use of plant parts—root, trunk, branches, leaves, fruit, pedicel, umbels, flowers, pith, veins, sap/juices, nodes, hairs—are essential descriptive criteria for identification and classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: identification and comparison require explicit attention to these parts and their characters (shape of leaves, structure of flowers and fruit, presence of hairs or pappus). The text enumerates these parts to show how plants differ and how such parts influence medicinal uses and classification.
